newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: YACHTING-MORNING GLORY BECALMED AS HEADS FOR RACE RECORD.
newsitem.headline: YACHTING-MORNING GLORY BECALMED AS HEADS FOR RACE RECORD.

text.p: German maxi Morning Glory regained the lead in the Sydney-to-Hobart overnight and was on schedule to break the 21-year race record on Saturday until she was becalmed off the east coast of Tasmania.
At the afternoon race schedule the 24.5 metre (80 foot) maxi was four hours inside the record with only 103 nautical miles to the finish line at Hobart, the capital of Tasmania.
But a lack of wind saw the maxi becalmed off Freycinet Peninsula on the mid-east Tasmanian coast, awaiting a forecast southerly change late on Saturday.
"We estimate Morning Glory should finish about 11.40 p.m. Saturday, but at this stage she is just sitting still," said a race official from Hobart.
"There is a forecast southerly change, but it depends when it arrives. If it is late, she may not finish until early Sunday," she said.
Morning Glory must cross the finish line by 3.36 a.m. (1636 GMT) on Sunday to break the race record of two days, 14 hours 36 minutes and 56 seconds set by U.S. maxi ketch Kialoa in 1975.

In second place in the 630 nautical mile race was Hong Kong pocket maxi Exile, 18 nautical miles astern of Morning Glory, with Australian maxi Amazon third a further three nautical miles behind. The original 95-boat fleet has been reduced to 80 because of equipment damage.

Sailing under spinnaker on Saturday morning in a 30-knot northeasterly tailwind, Morning Glory had a boat speed of around 15 knots -- a speed which would easily put the crew across the finish line on Saturday night. Ironically, Kialoa managed to only average 10 knots in its record-breaking run to Hobart.
But by the afternoon the wind had dropped off completely.
The Sydney-to-Hobart race record has stood for 21 years mainly because of the tricky winds off Tasmania's east coast and in the final run up the Derwent River to the finish.
In the past two years, the lead yacht has been well within the race record after charging down the east coast of Tasmania, only to be becalmed and robbed of the record.
"The Derwent is where the race record will be determined. It is in a wind shadow and it will all depend on conditions when the boats arrive on the river," said a race official.
If Morning Glory does break the record, the crew will collect A$300,000 (US$237,000), the richest prizemoney for a record-breaking line-honours win in a single ocean race.

A win and record by Morning Glory would also be remarkable comeback for the German maxi, which broke its mast only days before the start, forcing a frantic mission to fly a replacement mast from New Zealand in time for the start on Thursday.

Morning Glory was also one of 25 boats forced back to the starting line after a premature race beginning and then survived 40-knot southerly gales which snapped masts and shreaded sails of some of the other favourites only hours after the start.

The crew of Morning Glory have nursed their boat down the east Australian coast, at one stage sailing without a mainsail for fear of again snapping her mast, allowing pocket maxi Exile to take the lead on Friday.
But the larger Morning Glory regained the lead by Saturday, powered by her giant spinnaker and a 15-knot northeasterly tailwind.
